newsitem.title: USA: Japan's finance minister in New York.
newsitem.headline: Japan's finance minister in New York.

text.p: Japan's Finance Minister Wataru Kubo took time out from the IMF/World Bank meeting to visit New York on Monday and give his first public speech overseas, which may well be his last with elections looming.
"This may be the last time I will be speaking to you as a finance minister," he told the Japan Society, a non-profit organisation which promotes U.S.-Japan relations.

Kubo was in the United States to attend the Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers and central bankers meeting as well as the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. He slipped out of the ongoing international conferences in Washington to make his first speech overseas to a public audience.

Kubo, who belongs to the Social Democratic Party, does not need to be re-elected as a member of parliament because he belongs to the Upper House, not the Lower House which was dissolved on September 27 and faces elections on October 20.

But political analysts doubted his party could score a major win which would enable it to become a part of the next government. Socialists becamse increasingly unpopular after former socialist Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama played a major role in a government scheme to use public money to wind up troubled housing loan firms.

But Kubo noted in his speech that even if he lost his finance portfolio, the next government would continue the economic policies outlined by the current three-party coalition government headed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto of the largest Liberal Democratic Party.
Hashimoto's party was expected to remain in the government although it was not clear whether it would capture a simple majority or be forced to shop for new coalition partners.
Kubo said Japan would continue to pursue stable economic growth by pressing ahead with structural reforms, such as deregulation and formulating a deficit reduction plan.

He also defended the government's decision in April 1997 to raise the consumption tax to 5 percent from 3 percent to make up for previous tax cuts. He also said the special income tax cuts, worth two trillion yen ($18 billion), helped the economy move towards a recovery led by private-sector demand.

Kubo repeatedly said that the consumption tax would be raised as planned in light of tight state finances, despite the fact he was a major opponent of the tax when it was first introduced. As for special income tax cuts, Kubo said it was not yet time to decide. Analysts said continuance of such tax cuts will further bloat the state deficit.
But with elections looming, calls from politicians to freeze the consumption tax and maintain special income tax cuts were growing.
Even if the next government did not change its policies, Kubo might have to bow to pressures from his beleaguered party.
His party persuaded Takako Doi, the speaker of the house, to rejoin the Socialists as a leader, and she immediately began talking about reviewing the consumption tax hike.
Kubo told reporters that he would probably toe the party line should it decide to oppose the consumption tax hike.
